questions.q: What is the defining property of the identity matrix I, and what does it represent as a transformation?
options: I is the only matrix that cannot be multiplied by a vector
IM = MI = M for any compatible matrix M; as a transformation it represents 'do nothing,' leaving every vector unchanged
I always has determinant zero, representing a transformation that destroys all information
IM always equals the zero matrix, representing a transformation that erases M
questions.explain: The identity matrix leaves any compatible matrix (or vector) completely unchanged under multiplication, which is why it represents the 'do nothing' gate.

questions.q: For D = [[3,0],[0,-2]] and M = [[1,2],[3,4]], what is DM using the diagonal multiplication shortcut?
questions.explain: DM scales each ROW of M by the matching diagonal entry of D: row 1 (1,2) scaled by 3 gives (3,6); row 2 (3,4) scaled by -2 gives (-6,-8), so DM = [[3,6],[-6,-8]].

questions.q: Still using D = [[3,0],[0,-2]] and M = [[1,2],[3,4]], why does MD give a different result than DM?
options: Because DM scales the rows of M by D's diagonal entries, while MD scales the columns of M by D's diagonal entries -- these are different operations and generally give different results
They don't actually differ -- MD and DM are always equal for diagonal matrices
Because the problem statement contains a typo and MD is actually undefined
Because M and D have incompatible dimensions for one of the two orderings
questions.explain: Multiplying a diagonal matrix on the left scales rows of the other matrix; multiplying it on the right scales columns -- a direction-dependent operation that generally produces different results, matching DM=[[3,6],[-6,-8]] vs MD=[[3,-4],[9,-8]].

questions.q: For the block-diagonal matrix built from B1=[[1,2],[3,4]] and B2=[[0,1],[1,0]] applied to v=(1,1,1,0), why do the top two output entries depend only on B1 and the bottom two only on B2?
options: Blocks always mix in a block-diagonal matrix; this example is a special exception
Because B1 and B2 happen to contain identical numbers in this example, which coincidentally prevents mixing
Because the vector v was chosen specifically to force zero contributions from the off-diagonal zero entries
Because the off-diagonal blocks are all zero, so each block's rows only ever multiply against the slice of the vector that lines up with that block -- the blocks never mix
questions.explain: The zero entries outside the blocks guarantee that each block's row-times-column computation only ever involves its own slice of the vector, so B1 and B2 act completely independently.

questions.q: Why does the lesson connect block-diagonal matrices to multi-qubit quantum systems?
options: Because multi-qubit systems can only be described using diagonal matrices, never block matrices
Because every quantum gate matrix must be exactly block-diagonal with no exceptions
There is no real connection; it's just a coincidental mathematical analogy with no physical meaning

Because when gates act independently on separate qubits, the combined operation on the joint multi-qubit state has this same independent, non-mixing block structure -- previewing the tensor product covered in Chapter 6
questions.explain: Block-diagonal structure is numerically exactly what 'each subsystem transforms independently without affecting the other' looks like, which is the intuition behind combining separate qubits' gates via the tensor product.
